content: Listeriosis is a severe bacterial infection primarily caused by consuming contaminated food, such as unpasteurized dairy products or improperly packaged ready-to-eat foods. The emergence of listeriosis has been linked to changes in food consumption habits and advancements in food preservation technologies, such as refrigeration and vacuum packing of dairy, meat, and fish products. Among non-pregnant adults, the overall case-fatality rate is approximately 30%. In pregnant women, the infection can result in miscarriage, stillbirth, premature delivery, or neonatal infection. In young animals, the disease is often referred to as circling disease. Listeriosis is distributed worldwide and is caused by the bacterium Listeria monocytogenes. This bacterium is commonly found in soil, forage, water, mud, livestock feed, and silage. Animal reservoirs include infected domestic and wild mammals, birds, and humans. Animals can carry the bacterium asymptomatically and contaminate animal-origin foods, such as meat and dairy products. The disease is particularly severe in individuals with pre-existing debilitating conditions, such as organ transplantation, diabetes, cirrhosis, renal disease, heart disease, HIV infection, malignancies, or those on corticosteroids. Pregnant women are about 20 times more likely to contract listeriosis than other healthy adults. Neonates can acquire the infection if their mothers consume contaminated food during pregnancy. The primary mode of transmission is through the consumption of food contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes, including raw foods like uncooked meats and vegetables, as well as foods contaminated after cooking or processing, such as soft cheeses, smoked seafood, unpasteurized milk, and products made from unpasteurized milk. Neonatal infections can occur via transplacental transmission or during passage through an infected birth canal. The incubation period is uncertain but likely ranges from a few days to three weeks. Clinical manifestations vary depending on the type of infection and the host. In older adults and individuals with serious medical conditions, septicemia and meningitis are the most common presentations. Pregnant women may experience mild flu-like symptoms followed by fetal loss or neonatal meningitis. Immunocompetent individuals may develop acute gastroenteritis with high fever. Listeriosis is treatable with antibiotics. Preventive measures include maintaining clean and safe kitchen environments, thoroughly cooking meat and poultry, and safely storing foods. Individuals should avoid consuming raw milk or foods containing unpasteurized milk. Pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals should avoid ready-to-eat foods unless heated until steaming hot, smoked fish, and soft cheeses made with unpasteurized milk. Veterinarians and farmers should take precautions when handling aborted animal fetuses or sick/dead animals, particularly sheep that have died of encephalitis. Community-level prevention includes ensuring proper pasteurization of milk and dairy products, preventing post-pasteurization contamination, and avoiding the use of manure and sludge in vegetable farming. Melioidosis is a bacterial disease affecting humans and various animal species. The global movement of humans and animals has increased the potential for the disease to spread to new geographic areas. Clinical presentations vary by region, and the disease is underreported in many countries due to a lack of clinician awareness and laboratory capabilities. Mortality rates range from 40–75% despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy, with higher fatality rates in individuals with underlying diseases or immunosuppression. Melioidosis is endemic in Southeast Asia, China, and parts of Australia. It is caused by the bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, which is widespread in soil and muddy water in endemic areas, particularly in moist clay soils. Over 70% of cases occur in individuals with predisposing conditions such as diabetes, thalassemia, kidney disease, chronic lung disease, cancer, alcoholism, or steroid use. Agricultural, laboratory, and healthcare workers are at increased risk of occupational exposure. The disease is contracted through direct contact with contaminated soil and surface water. Infected animals can shed the bacterium through wounds, abscesses, nasal secretions, milk, feces, and urine. The incubation period ranges from one day to several months or even years. Some infections are asymptomatic, while others result in localized acute or chronic disease, or fatal septicemia. Common symptoms include abscesses of the salivary glands in children, acute localized infections at the site of inoculation, regional lymph node swelling, and lung disease, which is the most common form. Lung disease symptoms include fever, coughing, chest pain, and sometimes hemoptysis (coughing up blood). Septicemia is the most severe form, often occurring in individuals with pre-existing conditions such as diabetes, cancer, or kidney failure. Overwhelming infection can lead to death from septic shock within 48 hours of symptom onset. Treatment involves long-term antibiotic therapy, though success rates vary, and many drugs are ineffective against B. pseudomallei. The bacterium is susceptible to disinfectants such as 1% sodium hypochlorite, 70% ethanol, glutaraldehyde, and formaldehyde. Preventive measures include wearing gloves while gardening, promptly cleaning skin wounds, wearing boots during agricultural work, and using standard contact precautions (masks, gloves, gowns) in healthcare settings. Laboratory practices such as sniffing open culture plates should be avoided. Community-level prevention includes chlorination of water supplies and consuming only pasteurized dairy products. No vaccine is currently available. Plague, also known as the Black Death, is a rare but acute communicable disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It is primarily a rodent disease, with humans being incidental hosts. Historically, plague has caused widespread pandemics, resulting in up to 200 million deaths. It remains a life-threatening disease if not detected and treated early. Plague re-emerged in the 1990s in several countries and is classified as a re-emerging disease under the International Health Regulations (2005). Mortality rates depend on the type of plague: untreated bubonic plague is fatal in 50–75% of cases, but this decreases to 10–15% with treatment. Septicemic plague is almost always fatal without treatment, with a 40% fatality rate even with therapy. Pneumonic plague is fatal if untreated within 18–24 hours of infection. Plague is endemic in many countries in Africa, the Americas, and Asia, where it is maintained through flea–wild rodent–flea cycles. Contact between infected wild rodents and domestic rats can initiate urban cycles of spread. In the WHO Southeast Asia Region, endemic foci are found in India, Indonesia, and Myanmar. The primary vector is the rat flea, and rodents are the natural reservoirs of Y. pestis. At least 220 rodent species are known to be infected with the plague bacillus. Domestic rodents are highly susceptible to both infection and disease, leading to phenomena such as rat falls. Marmots are primary carriers in many Asian countries and, along with humans, can transmit pneumonic plague under normal circumstances. Dogs can become infected without showing symptoms and act as sentinel animals. Humans are at risk when they come into contact with rats in shared habitats. Pneumonic plague increases transmission efficiency through inhalation of aerosols. Geographic, meteorological, and climatic factors, as well as ecological changes caused by natural disasters, social advancement, and transportation activities, influence the distribution of rodent and insect reservoirs. Sociocultural factors, certain occupations, and lifestyles, such as hunting, cat ownership, sleeping on floors, and religious beliefs, also increase exposure risk. Plague can be transmitted indirectly through the bite of an infected flea (bubonic plague) or directly through contact with infected animals, human-to-human spread (pneumonic plague), or droplets contaminated with sputum. The incubation period is 2–6 days for bubonic plague and 1–4 days for pneumonic plague. Symptoms include flu-like signs such as fever, chills, headache, body aches, weakness, vomiting, and nausea. Clinical forms include bubonic (fever, swollen lymph nodes, meningitis), septicemic (fever, circulatory collapse, hemorrhagic rash), and pneumonic (fever, respiratory disease, bright red sputum). Rapid diagnosis and treatment with antibiotics are essential to reduce complications and fatality. Patients should be isolated during treatment. Preventive measures include prophylactic antibiotics, immunization for high-risk groups, rodent and flea control, effective sanitation, and public health education. Vaccines are not recommended for immediate outbreak protection.
